summary: A snapshot of the many RFCs that define and use IPsec and IKE, which come from numerous working groups, organized as a roadmap. It is informational.

eli5.summary: IPsec has grown into a huge pile of documents. This is a map telling you which one to read for what.

subtitle: A guide to the many RFCs that define, extend and use IPsec and IKE, as of February 2011.

tldr.problem: The number of RFCs defining and using IPsec and IKE had grown large, and they came from many IETF working groups, so it was hard to know which one applied.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a snapshot that lists each related RFC with a short description and its category and date, groups them by topic, and summarizes the requirement level of each cryptographic algorithm.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2411 and defines no requirements itself; if it conflicts with another RFC, the other RFC takes precedence.

today: RFC 6071 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2411. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, but it is a snapshot and states that its requirement levels are current as of February 2011.

sections.title: What the Roadmap Covers
sections.content:
IPsec is a suite of protocols that secures Internet communications at the IP layer. Its most common use is a Virtual Private Network (VPN), either gateway-to-gateway or between a remote user and an enterprise network. IKE is the key negotiation and management protocol most commonly used to supply keying material to IPsec. Both work with IPv4 and IPv6.

This roadmap obsoletes RFC 2411. Each listed RFC is tagged with its category: S for Standards Track, E for Experimental, B for Best Current Practice, and I for Informational, plus its publication date. The RFC does not define requirement levels. It restates those from the IKE and IPsec RFCs, current as of February 2011, and if it conflicts with any other RFC, the other RFC takes precedence.
sections.eli5: It is a table of contents for a very large library on one topic, with a one-line note on each book.

sections.title: How the Documents Fit Together
sections.content:
The main IPsec documents form seven groups: an Architecture document, an ESP document, an AH document, and sets of documents on encryption algorithms, combined-mode algorithms, integrity-protection algorithms, and IKE. ESP covers encryption and/or integrity protection; AH covers integrity protection and data-origin authentication.

Two versions of each protocol are in use. The "new" IPsec (IPsec-v3, from RFC 4301, RFC 4302 and RFC 4303) obsoleted the "old" IPsec (IPsec-v2), though IPsec-v2 is still commonly found in operational use. Likewise IKEv2 obsoleted IKEv1, which is also still commonly found.

IPsec-v3 changed how Security Associations are identified, added extended sequence numbers, added combined-mode algorithms, and made AH optional (MAY) where IPsec-v2 had it mandatory (MUST). IKEv2 replaced several exchange types with a single shorter exchange, made every request expect a response, added traffic selectors, and supports EAP-based authentication.
sections.eli5: There is an old edition and a new edition of each rulebook. Many places still use the old ones, so the map explains both.

sections.title: Base Documents and Extensions
sections.content:
For IPsec-v2 the base documents are RFC 2401 (architecture), RFC 2402 (AH) and RFC 2406 (ESP). For IPsec-v3 they are RFC 4301, 4302 and 4303. IPsec-v3 adds a Peer Authorization Database (PAD) that links IPsec to the key management protocol.

For IKEv1 the roadmap lists RFC 2409, ISAKMP (RFC 2408), the IPsec Domain of Interpretation (RFC 2407) and the Oakley description (RFC 2412). For IKEv2 it lists RFC 4306, the clarifications in RFC 4718, and RFC 5996, which combines the first two and resolves further implementation issues.

Extensions are grouped by topic: NAT traversal and UDP encapsulation of ESP (RFC 3947, 3948), extended sequence numbers, opportunistic encryption, extra peer authentication methods such as repeated, multiple or EAP-only authentication and ECDSA, certificate profiles, dead peer detection, and remote access features such as MOBIKE, session resumption and gateway redirect.
sections.eli5: The map first lists the main rulebooks, then the add-on booklets sorted by what each one helps with, such as getting through home routers or staying connected while moving.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithms and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
An algorithm can be used in IKE or IPsec only if it has an IANA value and an RFC that says how to use it in the protocol. For each algorithm RFC the roadmap records a requirement level for IKEv1, IKEv2, IPsec-v2 and IPsec-v3: MUST, SHOULD, MAY, the variants SHOULD+, SHOULD- and MUST-, "optional", "undefined" or "N/A". Appendix A summarizes them.

The levels themselves live in separate RFCs: RFC 4835 for ESP and AH, RFC 4307 for IKEv2 and RFC 4109 for IKEv1. The roadmap then walks through encryption, integrity, combined-mode and pseudo-random function RFCs, cryptographic suites, and Diffie-Hellman groups, including RFC 5903, which obsoletes RFC 4753.

One example: for AES-CBC with 128-bit keys the levels are SHOULD for IKEv1, SHOULD+ for IKEv2, and MUST for both ESP-v2 and ESP-v3.
sections.eli5: Each cipher gets a label for each edition: must have, should have, or optional. It is like a packing list that says which items are required for the trip.

sections.title: Multicast, Outgrowths and Other Users
sections.content:
Classical IPsec SAs are point-to-point, so the Multicast Security working group defined alternatives to IKE and extensions to IPsec for multicast, including the Group Domain of Interpretation (RFC 3547) and RFC 5374.

The roadmap also lists outgrowths of IPsec and IKE: policy, MIBs, IP payload compression (IPComp), Better-Than-Nothing Security, Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys, IPsec Secure Remote Access and keys in DNS. It notes that some of these, such as RFC 3585 and RFC 4807, have not been widely adopted.

Other protocols use IPsec or IKE, among them Mobile IP, OSPF, Host Identity Protocol, SCTP, Robust Header Compression, BGP, NAT, and SIP. Others adapt IKEv2 for non-IPsec functions: EAP-IKEv2, Fibre Channel and a wireless radio-link product.
sections.eli5: The last chapters of the map point to side roads: sending to many receivers at once, extra features, and other systems that borrow IPsec's locks.
